subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 57-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction is advised to take low-dose aspirin daily. Aspirin acetylates a serine residue in the cyclooxygenase active site of platelet prostaglandin H2 synthase. Platelet aggregation remains impaired for the life of the platelet, approximately 7 to 10 days, even though aspirin is cleared from the plasma within a few hours.
question: Which of the following best characterizes aspirin's inhibition of cyclooxygenase?

options.text: Reversible competitive inhibition that can be overcome by increasing arachidonic acid concentration
Irreversible mechanism-based (suicide) inhibition produced by covalent modification of the enzyme
Uncompetitive inhibition that requires formation of the enzyme-substrate complex
Reversible allosteric inhibition that lowers Vmax without changing Km
Feedback inhibition of cyclooxygenase by its own prostaglandin products

explanation_correct: Aspirin transfers its acetyl group covalently to a serine residue in the cyclooxygenase active site, which irreversibly inactivates the enzyme and is a classic example of suicide (mechanism-based) inhibition. Because platelets cannot synthesize new protein, enzyme activity returns only when new platelets are produced, roughly 7 to 10 days after the last dose. This is why low-dose aspirin produces a prolonged antiplatelet effect despite its short plasma half-life.

explanation_incorrect.A: Competitive inhibition is reversible and would be overcome by higher arachidonic acid concentrations; aspirin's acetylation cannot be reversed by substrate.
explanation_incorrect.C: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme-substrate complex and reduce both Km and Vmax; aspirin permanently inactivates the enzyme through covalent chemistry.
explanation_incorrect.D: Allosteric inhibitors are typically reversible, and aspirin's stable covalent mark on the enzyme accounts for the prolonged effect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Product feedback inhibition is reversible and does not explain the week-long platelet defect after a single dose.

educationalObjective: Aspirin is a suicide (irreversible) inhibitor that acetylates cyclooxygenase covalently, so its antiplatelet effect lasts for the lifespan of the platelet.
